title: Supreme Court upholds Tennessee ban on gender-affirming care for minors - NewsBreak
text: WASHINGTON (NEXSTAR) – The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday upheld a Tennessee law banning gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors, a decision that could have widespread implications for families across the country. The 6-3 ruling allows Tennessee, and potentially more than 20 other states, to enforce bans on treatments such as puberty blockers and hormone therapy for transgender youth. Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti, who defended the law in court, welcomed the decision. “Evidence continues to come in showing that this is not an appropriate treatment for kids,” Skrmetti said, adding, “The real scandal is how we got to this point.” Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley also praised the ruling. “These are kids. They come in with often mental health issues, they’re feeling depressed, and doctors say, what needs to happen is a gender transition surgery,” Hawley said. “This is common sense.” Writing for the majority, Chief Justice John Roberts said the case did not violate the Constitution’s Equal Protection Clause. He emphasized that the issue involved complex scientific and policy debates, which should be left to the states. Democrats harshly criticized the decision. “It’s an awful decision,” said Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, (D-N.Y.). “The Supreme Court has forgotten that one of its jobs is to protect individual rights.” In her dissent, Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote that the court “abandons transgender children and their families to political whims,” calling the decision a failure of proper judicial review. The American Civil Liberties Union, which brought the case on behalf of affected families, warned the ruling could force thousands to leave their home states to seek medical care elsewhere. “It’s devastating for the people who are most affected,” said Chase Strangio, an attorney with the ACLU. Medical groups, including the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics, oppose such bans. They argue that gender-affirming care, when appropriately administered, can be life-saving. The ruling marks a significant setback for advocates of transgender rights and leaves the future of youth gender care policy in the hands of state governments.
